items.stem: Which term describes a definition based on the content of religious belief, such as belief in God or the supernatural?
items.answer: Substantive definition of religion
items.markingKey: Substantive definition of religion: a definition based on the content of religious belief, such as belief in God or the supernatural. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “substantive definition of religion”, and give one example.
items.answer: A definition based on the content of religious belief, such as belief in God or the supernatural. Example: Weber’s focus on belief in a superior power.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (a definition based on the content of religious belief, such as belief in God or the supernatural); 1 mark for a relevant example such as Weber’s focus on belief in a superior power. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “functional definition of religion” and “social constructionist definition of religion”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Functional definition of religion: a definition based on what religion does for individuals or society, such as creating solidarity (e.g. Durkheim’s view of religion as uniting a moral community). Social constructionist definition of religion: a definition that focuses on how members of society themselves define what counts as religion (e.g. debates over whether a new movement is a “real” religion).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Fans of a football club in Manila gather every week, sing songs together, treat the stadium as a sacred place and mourn former players with rituals. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: in a pick-and-mix society the boundaries of religion are blurred; personal spiritual and secular beliefs mix.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Fans of a football club in Mumbai gather every week, sing songs together, treat the stadium as a sacred place and mourn former players with rituals. Explain how a Weberian sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religion should be defined by its content: belief in a superior or supernatural power (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research the number of people who describe themselves as religious.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the number of people who describe themselves as religious but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “social constructionist definition of religion”.

items.stem: What is the difference between “functional definition of religion” and “sacred”?
items.answer: Functional definition of religion: a definition based on what religion does for individuals or society, such as creating solidarity. Sacred: things set apart and forbidden, which inspire awe and reverence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “sacred” and “profane”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Sacred: things set apart and forbidden, which inspire awe and reverence (e.g. a holy book or temple). Profane: ordinary, everyday things with no special significance (e.g. a household chair).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Cape Town wants to research how members of new movements define their beliefs. Explain one limitation of using case studies for this research.
items.answer: The detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases.

items.stem: Fans of a football club in Colombo gather every week, sing songs together, treat the stadium as a sacred place and mourn former players with rituals. Compare how functionalist and postmodernist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: religion should be defined by its functions: anything that creates solidarity and shared sacred values may count (Durkheim). Postmodernism: in a pick-and-mix society the boundaries of religion are blurred; personal spiritual and secular beliefs mix.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A survey of 200 adults in Cairo asked what makes a person religious, and which features applied to them. Table: adults agreeing (%) | Say this makes a person religious | Say this applies to them. Belief in God | 85% | 51%. Belief in a spiritual force but not God | 36% | 22%. Belong to a religious group | 65% | 37%. Practise rituals at home | 47% | 42%. (a) Calculate the difference between Belief in a spiritual force but not God and Belong to a religious group for Say this makes a person religious and for Say this applies to them, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that how religion is defined affects how religious a society appears.
items.answer: (a) Say this makes a person religious: 29 percentage points; Say this applies to them: 15 percentage points; the difference is larger for Say this makes a person religious. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Say this applies to them than for Say this makes a person religious among Belief in God, Belief in a spiritual force but not God, Belong to a religious group, Practise rituals at home; Belief in God had the highest figure for Say this applies to them. Definitions of religion differ between individuals. Qualifications: Closed questions may not capture complex views; one city may be untypical; social desirability may affect answers. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 200 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (29 and 15); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how people practise religion privately. Evaluate the use of participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it can give access to groups that would never complete a questionnaire, such as deviant subcultures; the researcher sees what people actually do in their natural setting, not just what they say, so validity is high. Limitations: it is very difficult to observe private behaviour inside homes; studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how people practise religion privately but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Leila compared national surveys of 800 adults in a country near Mumbai. Table: adults in each category (%) | 1990 | 2020. Believe in God | 72% | 61%. Belong to a religious group | 65% | 47%. Attend services at least monthly | 27% | 19%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Attend services at least monthly between 1990 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that believing without belonging explains the decline in attendance.
items.answer: (a) 19 − 27 = -8 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for Believe in God, Belong to a religious group, Attend services at least monthly; Believe in God had the highest figure for 2020. Belief has declined more slowly than practice (believing without belonging). Qualifications: Belief has also fallen; surveys rely on self-report; question wording may differ between years; spirituality may be missed. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 800 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 27 and 19; 1 mark for -8 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research changes in religious attendance over time.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in religious attendance over time but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: A wellness centre in Lagos offers mindfulness, reiki and sound healing; it is busier on Sunday mornings than the church next door. Compare how Weberian and functionalist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religious ideas can bring about social change; beliefs such as the Protestant ethic shaped economic behaviour, and religion can motivate social movements (Weber). Functionalism: religion promotes social solidarity and value consensus, helps people cope with life crises and reinforces the collective conscience (Durkheim, Malinowski, Parsons).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using participant observation to research why people take part in holistic spirituality.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; it is often the only way to study small or closed groups in depth. Limitations: studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise; the researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”). Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why people take part in holistic spirituality but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

What is the difference, in percentage points, between Say this makes a person religious and Say this applies to them for Belief in a spiritual force but not God (Say this applies to them minus Say this makes a person religious)?
items.answer: -14 percentage points
items.markingKey: 18 − 32 = -14 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A survey of 300 adults in Colombo asked what makes a person religious, and which features applied to them. Table: adults agreeing (%) | Say this makes a person religious | Say this applies to them. Belief in God | 75% | 41%. Belief in a spiritual force but not God | 33% | 20%. Belong to a religious group | 63% | 41%. Practise rituals at home | 42% | 36%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Say this makes a person religious and Say this applies to them for Practise rituals at home. (b) Calculate the difference between Practise rituals at home and Belong to a religious group for Say this makes a person religious and for Say this applies to them, and state for which of these the difference is larger.
items.answer: (a) 36 − 42 = -6 percentage points (Say this applies to them compared with Say this makes a person religious). (b) Say this makes a person religious: 21 percentage points; Say this applies to them: 5 percentage points; the difference is larger for Say this makes a person religious.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 42 and 36; 1 mark for 6 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark each difference (21 and 5); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3]

items.stem: A new movement in Madrid meets weekly, follows a leader’s teachings about personal growth and holds ceremonies, but has no belief in God; the government refuses to register it as a religion. Explain how a Weberian sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religion should be defined by its content: belief in a superior or supernatural power (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful official statistics are for studying the number of people who describe themselves as religious.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them; definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the number of people who describe themselves as religious but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Ines surveyed 1200 adults about how they define religion. Table: adults agreeing (%) | Say this makes a person religious | Say this applies to them. Belief in God | 82% | 46%. Belief in a spiritual force but not God | 36% | 29%. Belong to a religious group | 57% | 37%. Practise rituals at home | 43% | 35%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Say this makes a person religious and Say this applies to them for Belong to a religious group. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of definitions of religion. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that how religion is defined affects how religious a society appears.
items.answer: (a) 37 − 57 = -20 percentage points (Say this applies to them compared with Say this makes a person religious). (b) Response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Say this applies to them than for Say this makes a person religious among Belief in God, Belief in a spiritual force but not God, Belong to a religious group, Practise rituals at home; Belief in God had the highest figure for Say this applies to them. Many people hold beliefs without belonging. Qualifications: Closed questions may not capture complex views; one city may be untypical; social desirability may affect answers. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 1200 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 57 and 37; 1 mark for 20 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes membership of, or identification with, a religious organisation?
items.answer: Religious belonging
items.markingKey: Religious belonging: membership of, or identification with, a religious organisation. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “religious belief”.
items.answer: What people believe about God, the supernatural or the afterlife.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: what people believe about God, the supernatural or the afterlife. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “operationalisation” and “religious belonging”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Operationalisation: turning a concept into something that can be measured (e.g. measuring religiosity by counting weekly attendance). Religious belonging: membership of, or identification with, a religious organisation (e.g. being a registered member of a church).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In a census in Manila, 70% of people state a religion, but only 9% attend a religious service in a typical week. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: participation in shared rituals is what matters, because religion’s function is to create solidarity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Leila compared national surveys of 300 adults in a country near Bogotá. Table: adults in each category (%) | 1990 | 2020. Believe in God | 74% | 56%. Belong to a religious group | 60% | 44%. Attend services at least monthly | 22% | 10%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Believe in God change between 1990 and 2020?
items.answer: -18 percentage points
items.markingKey: 56 − 74 = -18 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Sofia compared national surveys of 200 adults in a country near Lisbon. Table: adults in each category (%) | 1990 | 2020. Believe in God | 65% | 51%. Belong to a religious group | 63% | 43%. Attend services at least monthly | 25% | 15%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Attend services at least monthly between 1990 and 2020. Show your working. (b) Calculate the gap between Attend services at least monthly and Believe in God in 1990 and in 2020, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (c) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of belief, belonging and practice.
items.answer: (a) (15 − 25) ÷ 25 × 100 = -40%. (b) 1990: 40 percentage points; 2020: 36 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (c) They measure what people say they do, not what they actually do.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (15 − 25) ÷ 25 × 100; 1 mark for -40% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark each gap (40 and 36); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (c) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2]

items.stem: Two national surveys, each of 1000 adults, produced the results below. Table: adults in each category (%) | 1990 | 2020. Believe in God | 67% | 55%. Belong to a religious group | 57% | 37%. Attend services at least monthly | 26% | 15%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Believe in God between 1990 and 2020. (b) Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that believing without belonging explains the decline in attendance.
items.answer: (a) 55 − 67 = -12 percentage points. (b) They measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure fell for Believe in God, Belong to a religious group, Attend services at least monthly; Believe in God had the highest figure for 2020. Religion has become more private. Qualifications: Belief has also fallen; surveys rely on self-report; question wording may differ between years; spirituality may be missed. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 1000 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 67 and 55; 1 mark for -12 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a diverse set of beliefs and practices focusing on self-spirituality and personal growth?
items.answer: New Age
items.markingKey: New Age: a diverse set of beliefs and practices focusing on self-spirituality and personal growth. [1]

items.stem: Briefly explain Bruce’s view that spirituality is a sign of secularisation, not religious revival.
items.answer: Bruce argued New Age beliefs are weak, individual and have little social significance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Bruce argued New Age beliefs are weak, individual and have little social significance. [2]

items.stem: Lyon argued that religion has relocated to the sphere of consumption in a postmodern “Jesus in Disneyland”. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Lyon argued people consume religion as part of a pick-and-mix lifestyle. Criticism: Many people still belong to traditional religions.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Postmodernism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Surveys of 800 adults in Karachi in two years produced the results below. Table: adults (%) | 2000 | 2020. Attend religious services weekly | 17% | 12%. Practise meditation or yoga weekly | 5% | 10%. Describe themselves as “spiritual but not religious” | 10% | 24%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Describe themselves as “spiritual but not religious” change between 2000 and 2020?
items.answer: +14 percentage points
items.markingKey: 24 − 10 = +14 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Isla compared surveys of 1000 adults about religion and spirituality. Table: adults (%) | 2000 | 2020. Attend religious services weekly | 17% | 13%. Practise meditation or yoga weekly | 6% | 14%. Describe themselves as “spiritual but not religious” | 8% | 21%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Attend religious services weekly between 2000 and 2020. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that a spiritual revolution is taking place.
items.answer: (a) 13 − 17 = -4 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Practise meditation or yoga weekly, Describe themselves as “spiritual but not religious”; the figure fell for Attend religious services weekly; Describe themselves as “spiritual but not religious” had the highest figure for 2020. Consumer culture and the wellness industry. Qualifications: Yoga may be exercise rather than spirituality; numbers remain smaller than religious attendance; self-description may be vague. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 1000 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 17 and 13; 1 mark for -4 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]
